question: According to the Wyoming CDL Manual, what is the most important reason for inspecting your commercial vehicle?
choice_a: Safety, for yourself and other road users
choice_b: To avoid a citation from law enforcement
choice_c: To keep the vehicle's resale value high
choice_d: To satisfy the motor carrier's insurance company
explanation: The manual states, "Safety is the most important reason you inspect your vehicle, safety for yourself and for other road users."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.1.1 Why Inspect

question: The Wyoming CDL Manual describes which three types of vehicle inspection a driver should perform?
choice_a: Pre-trip, mid-trip radio check, and annual DOT inspection
choice_b: Pre-trip inspection, inspection during the trip, and after-trip inspection and report
choice_c: Morning inspection, noon inspection, and evening inspection
choice_d: Only a pre-trip inspection is required
explanation: The manual organizes vehicle inspection into a Pre-Trip Inspection, checks During a Trip, and an After-trip Inspection and Report.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.1.2 Types of Vehicle Inspection

question: Per the Wyoming CDL Manual, what is the minimum tread depth required on front tires versus other tires?
choice_a: 2/32 inch on front tires, 4/32 inch on other tires
choice_b: 4/32 inch on all tires
choice_c: 4/32 inch on front tires, 2/32 inch on other tires
choice_d: 6/32 inch on front tires, 4/32 inch on other tires
explanation: The manual states, "You need at least 4/32-inch tread depth in every major groove on front tires. You need 2/32 inch on other tires."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.1.3 What to Look For - Tire Problems

question: How much steering wheel play can make a vehicle hard to steer, according to the manual?
choice_a: Any play at all
choice_b: More than 2 degrees
choice_c: More than 5 degrees
choice_d: More than 10 degrees (about two inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch steering wheel)
explanation: The manual warns that "Steering wheel play of more than 10 degrees (approximately two inches movement at the rim of a 20-inch steering wheel) can make it hard to steer."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.1.3 What to Look For - Steering System Defects

question: Under the Wyoming CDL Manual, when should a leaf spring defect put a vehicle 'out of service'?
choice_a: If one-fourth or more of the leaves are missing in a leaf spring
choice_b: If any single leaf is scratched
choice_c: If the spring is more than five years old
choice_d: Only if the entire spring assembly is detached
explanation: The manual states, "Missing or broken leaves in any leaf spring. If one-fourth or more are missing, it will put the vehicle 'out of service.'"
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.1.3 What to Look For - Suspension System Defects

question: During Step 3 of the seven-step inspection (starting the engine and checking gauges), how quickly should air pressure build from 50 to 90 psi?
choice_a: Within thirty seconds
choice_b: Within three minutes
choice_c: Within ten minutes
choice_d: It should never change once the engine starts
explanation: The manual states, "Air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within three minutes."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.1.5 Step 3: Start Engine and Inspect Inside the Cab

question: The Wyoming CDL Manual says air pressure should build to a governor cut-out usually around what range?
explanation: The manual notes to "Build air pressure to governor cut-out usually around 120-140 psi."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.1.5 Step 3: Start Engine and Inspect Inside the Cab

question: In Step 7 of the pre-trip inspection, how do you test a hydraulic brake system for leaks?
choice_a: Pump the pedal once and release it immediately
choice_b: Rev the engine to 2,000 rpm and watch the brake warning light
choice_c: Drive the vehicle at 5 mph and apply the brake firmly, checking for pulling
choice_d: Pump the brake pedal three times, then apply firm pressure and hold it for five seconds; the pedal should not move
explanation: The manual instructs: "pump the brake pedal three times. Then apply firm pressure to the pedal and hold for five seconds. The pedal should not move."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.1.5 Step 7: Start the Engine and Check

question: Drivers of trucks and truck tractors transporting cargo must inspect the securement of the cargo within the first how many miles of a trip, and how often after that?
choice_a: Within the first 50 miles, then every 150 miles or every three hours, whichever comes first
choice_b: Within the first 100 miles, then every 500 miles
choice_c: Within the first 10 miles, then every hour
choice_d: Only once, before departure
explanation: The manual states drivers "must inspect the securement of the cargo within the first 50 miles of a trip and every 150 miles or every three hours (whichever comes first) after."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.1.6 Inspection During a Trip - Safety Inspection

question: Why does the Wyoming CDL Manual recommend backing and turning toward the driver's side whenever possible?
choice_a: It is required by federal law in all states
choice_b: It lets you see better by looking out the side window, since backing toward the right side is very dangerous because you can't see as well
choice_c: It reduces wear on the right rear tires
choice_d: It is the only way to activate backup alarms
explanation: The manual says to "Back to the driver's side so you can see better. Backing toward the right side is very dangerous because you can't see as well."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: According to the manual, how should you back a commercial vehicle?
choice_a: As quickly as possible to minimize time in the blind spot
choice_b: In neutral, coasting
choice_c: As slowly as possible, using the lowest reverse gear, so you can correct steering errors and stop quickly if needed
choice_d: In the highest reverse gear available for better control
explanation: The manual advises, "Always back as slowly as possible. Use the lowest reverse gear. That way you can more easily correct any steering errors. You also can stop quickly if necessary."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: When starting a manual-transmission vehicle on a grade, when should you release the parking brake?
choice_a: As soon as the clutch is engaged, regardless of engine power
choice_b: Immediately after starting the engine
choice_c: Only after shifting into second gear
choice_d: Only after you have applied enough engine power to keep the vehicle from rolling back
explanation: The manual states, "Release the parking brake only when you have applied enough engine power to keep from rolling back."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.2.1 Accelerating

question: If you have a manual transmission, when should you push the clutch in while stopping?
choice_a: When the engine is close to idle
choice_b: As soon as you begin braking
choice_c: Only after the vehicle has fully stopped
choice_d: Never; leave it engaged the whole time
explanation: The manual states, "If you have a manual transmission, push the clutch in when the engine is close to idle."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.2.3 Stopping

question: According to the manual, which vehicles require double clutching to change gears?
choice_a: All automatic transmission vehicles
choice_b: Most heavy vehicles with un-synchronized manual transmissions; double clutching is NOT required with a synchronized manual transmission
choice_c: Only vehicles with retarders
choice_d: Only vehicles pulling doubles or triples
explanation: The manual states, "Most heavy vehicles with un-synchronized manual transmissions require double clutching to change gears. If equipped with a synchronized manual transmission, double clutching is NOT required."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions

question: What does the manual advise about shifting down before starting down a hill?
choice_a: Wait until your speed has already built up, then downshift for maximum control
choice_b: Downshifting before a hill is unnecessary if you have good brakes
choice_c: Slow down and shift down before starting down the hill, to a speed you can control without using the brakes hard
choice_d: Always use the same gear you would use to climb the identical hill, regardless of vehicle type
explanation: The manual instructs, "Slow down and shift down to a speed that you can control without using the brakes hard. Otherwise the brakes can overheat and lose their braking power."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.3.1 Basic Procedures for Shifting Down

question: When should you turn off a vehicle's retarder, according to the Wyoming CDL Manual?
choice_a: Whenever traveling above 40 mph
choice_b: Whenever pulling a loaded trailer
choice_c: Only when parked
choice_d: Whenever the road is wet, icy, or snow covered, because poor traction can let the retarder cause the drive wheels to skid
explanation: The manual warns, "When your drive wheels have poor traction, the retarder may cause them to skid. Therefore, you should turn the retarder off whenever the road is wet, icy, or snow covered."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.3.4 Retarders

question: Why would a driver select a low range on an automatic transmission when going down a grade?
choice_a: To get greater engine braking, since lower ranges prevent the transmission from shifting up beyond the selected gear
choice_b: To increase fuel economy on flat roads
choice_c: To automatically engage the parking brake
choice_d: To disable the retarder
explanation: The manual states you "can select a low range to get greater engine braking when going down grades. The lower ranges prevent the transmission from shifting up beyond the selected gear."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.3.3 Automatic Transmissions

question: How many basic types of retarders does the Wyoming CDL Manual describe?
choice_a: Two (engine and exhaust only)
choice_b: Four (exhaust, engine, hydraulic, and electric)
choice_c: Six
choice_d: Retarders are not categorized into types
explanation: The manual states, "There are four basic types of retarders (exhaust, engine, hydraulic, and electric)."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.3.4 Retarders

question: Most good drivers look how far ahead, according to the manual?
choice_a: 5 to 8 seconds ahead
choice_b: 20 to 25 seconds ahead
choice_c: 12 to 15 seconds ahead
choice_d: Only as far as the vehicle directly in front
explanation: The manual states, "Most good drivers look at least 12 to 15 seconds ahead."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.4.1 Seeing Ahead

question: At highway speeds, about how far is the distance you would travel looking 12 to 15 seconds ahead?
choice_a: About 100 feet
choice_b: About one city block
choice_c: About one mile
choice_d: About a quarter of a mile
explanation: The manual states that at highway speeds, 12-15 seconds ahead "is about a quarter of a mile," while at lower/city speeds it is about one city block.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.4.1 Seeing Ahead, Figure 2.6

question: What does the manual warn about convex ('fisheye' or 'spot') mirrors?
choice_a: Everything appears smaller and farther away than it really is
choice_b: They eliminate all blind spots completely
choice_c: They must be replaced with flat mirrors before driving
choice_d: They only work properly at night
explanation: The manual notes "everything appears smaller in a convex mirror than it would if you were looking at it directly. Things also seem farther away than they really are."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.4.2 Seeing to the Sides and Rear, Figure 2.7

question: When can mirror adjustment be checked most accurately, according to the manual?
choice_a: Only while the vehicle is in motion
choice_b: When the trailer(s) are straight
choice_c: Only during a full stop with the engine off
choice_d: It cannot be checked accurately; mirrors should just be factory-set
explanation: The manual states, "Mirror adjustment should be checked prior to the start of any trip and can only be checked accurately when the trailer(s) are straight."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.4.2 Seeing to the Sides and Rear - Mirror Adjustment

question: Which of the following is one of the manual's three rules for using turn signals?
choice_a: Cancel the signal before completing the turn to avoid confusing other drivers
choice_b: Only signal if another vehicle is visible behind you
choice_c: Signal early, well before you turn, to keep others from trying to pass you
choice_d: Signal only for left turns; right turns don't require signaling
explanation: The manual's rules for turn signals include, "Signal early. Signal well before you turn. It is the best way to keep others from trying to pass you."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.5.1 Signal Your Intentions - Turns

question: If you must stop on or by a one-way or divided highway, where should you place your warning triangles?
choice_a: 5 feet, 50 feet, and 100 feet toward approaching traffic
choice_b: All three within 10 feet of the vehicle
choice_c: 20 feet, 150 feet, and 300 feet toward approaching traffic
choice_d: 10 feet, 100 feet, and 200 feet toward the approaching traffic
explanation: The manual states, "If you must stop on or by a one-way or divided highway, place warning devices 10 feet, 100 feet, and 200 feet toward the approaching traffic."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.5.2 Communicating Your Presence, Figure 2.8

question: On a two-lane road carrying traffic in both directions, how should warning devices be placed after stopping?
choice_a: Within 10 feet of the front or rear corners of the vehicle, and 100 feet behind and ahead of the vehicle
choice_b: Only 200 feet behind the vehicle
choice_c: In a straight line directly behind the vehicle, spaced 5 feet apart
choice_d: There is no requirement on two-way roads
explanation: The manual states to "place warning devices within 10 feet of the front or rear corners to mark the location of the vehicle and 100 feet behind and ahead of the vehicle."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.5.2 Communicating Your Presence, Figure 2.9

question: If you must stop on a road or shoulder, within how many minutes must you put out your emergency warning devices?
choice_a: Five minutes
choice_b: Ten minutes
choice_c: Thirty minutes
choice_d: There is no time limit as long as flashers are on
explanation: The manual states, "you must put out your emergency warning devices within ten minutes."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.5.2 Communicating Your Presence

question: At 55 mph, about how many feet does the average alert driver travel during perception time (1-3/4 seconds)?
choice_a: 61 feet
choice_b: 216 feet
choice_c: 419 feet
choice_d: 142 feet
explanation: The manual states, "The average perception time for an alert driver is 1-3/4 seconds. At 55 mph this accounts for 142 feet traveled."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.6.1 Stopping Distance - Perception Distance

question: At 55 mph, the average driver's reaction distance (1/2 to 1 second reaction time) is about how many feet?
choice_a: 61 feet
choice_b: 142 feet
choice_c: 216 feet
choice_d: 419 feet
explanation: The manual states, "The average driver has a reaction time of 1/2 second to 1 second. At 55 mph this accounts for 61 feet traveled."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.6.1 Stopping Distance - Reaction Distance

question: At 55 mph on dry pavement with good brakes, what is the total minimum stopping distance described in the manual?
choice_a: About 216 feet
choice_b: About 419 feet
choice_c: About 142 feet
choice_d: About 61 feet
explanation: The manual states, "At 55 mph, your vehicle will travel a minimum of 419 feet" when perception, reaction, and braking distances are combined.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.6.1 Stopping Distance - Total Stopping Distance, Figure 2.11

topic: Effect of doubling speed on stopping distance
question: According to the manual, when you double your speed from 20 to 40 mph, how much greater is the impact and braking distance?
choice_a: 2 times greater
choice_b: 3 times greater
choice_c: 4 times greater
choice_d: 9 times greater
explanation: The manual states, "When you double your speed from 20 to 40 mph the impact is 4 times greater. The braking distance is also 4 times longer."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.6.1 The Effect of Speed on Stopping Distance

question: How much should you reduce your speed on a wet road, per the manual's example (such as slowing from 55 mph)?
choice_a: By about one-tenth
choice_b: By about three-fourths
choice_c: To a complete crawl
choice_d: By about one-third (e.g., slow from 55 to about 35 mph)
explanation: The manual advises, "Reduce speed by about one-third (e.g., slow from 55 to about 35 mph) on a wet road."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.6.2 Matching Speed to the Road Surface - Slippery Surfaces

question: According to the manual, hydroplaning can occur at speeds as low as what, if there is a lot of water on the road?
choice_a: 30 mph
choice_b: 45 mph
choice_c: 55 mph
choice_d: 65 mph
explanation: The manual states, "Hydroplaning can occur at speeds as low as 30 mph if there is a lot of water."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.6.2 Identifying Slippery Surfaces - Hydroplaning

question: What is the basic rule of thumb for following distance given in the manual, for speeds under 40 mph?
choice_a: One second for every 5 feet of vehicle length
choice_b: One second for each 10 feet of vehicle length
choice_c: Two seconds regardless of vehicle length
choice_d: One second for every 20 feet of vehicle length
explanation: The manual states, "One good rule says you need at least one second for each 10 feet of vehicle length at speeds below 40 mph."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.7.1 Space Ahead - How Much Space?

question: For a 40-foot vehicle traveling above 40 mph, how many seconds of following distance does the manual's example call for?
choice_a: Three seconds
choice_b: Four seconds
choice_c: Five seconds
choice_d: Seven seconds
explanation: The manual states that above 40 mph you must add a second for safety, giving "five seconds for a 40-foot vehicle."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.7.1 Space Ahead, Figure 2.12

question: If you are being tailgated, what does the manual advise you to do?
choice_a: Speed up to put distance between you and the tailgater
choice_b: Flash your brake lights repeatedly to warn them off
choice_c: Turn on your taillights as a signal to back off
choice_d: Avoid quick changes, increase your following distance, and don't speed up
explanation: The manual's tips include avoiding quick changes, increasing following distance, and not speeding up, since "it's safer to be tailgated at a low speed than a high speed."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.7.2 Space Behind - Dealing with Tailgaters Safely

question: When making a right turn in a vehicle that cannot complete it without swinging into another lane, what does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Turn wide as you complete the turn, keeping the rear of the vehicle close to the curb
choice_b: Swing wide to the left before starting the turn to gain clearance
choice_c: Straddle both lanes throughout the entire turn
choice_d: Back up if a vehicle is coming the other way
explanation: The manual advises to "turn wide as you complete the turn. Keep the rear of your vehicle close to the curb. This will stop other drivers from passing you on the right."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.7.6 Space for Turns - Right Turns

question: On a left turn, what does the manual say you should do before starting the turn?
choice_a: Begin turning as soon as you enter the intersection
choice_b: Make sure you have reached the center of the intersection before you start the left turn
choice_c: Always use the inside (left) turn lane if two turn lanes are present
choice_d: Straddle the centerline the entire time
explanation: The manual states, "On a left turn, make sure you have reached the center of the intersection before you start the left turn. If you turn too soon, the left side of your vehicle may hit another vehicle because of off tracking."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.7.6 Space for Turns - Left Turns

topic: Space below - railroad tracks and depressions
question: What does the manual warn about crossing railroad tracks or drainage channels with a heavily loaded vehicle?
choice_a: They pose no risk since vehicles are built with enough ground clearance
choice_b: Only empty vehicles are at risk of getting hung up
choice_c: The ends of the vehicle can drag or get hung up, so such depressions should be crossed carefully
choice_d: You should always accelerate quickly to clear them
explanation: The manual states, "Drainage channels across roads can cause the ends of some vehicles to drag. Cross such depressions carefully," and warns about railroad tracks hanging up trailers with low clearance.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.7.5 Space Below

question: How does the Wyoming CDL Manual define a 'hazard'?
choice_a: Only a mechanical defect on your own vehicle
choice_b: Any citation issued by law enforcement
choice_c: Exclusively bad weather conditions
choice_d: Any road condition or other road user that is a possible danger
explanation: The manual states, "A hazard is any road condition or other road user (driver, bicyclist, pedestrian) that is a possible danger."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.8.1 Importance of Seeing Hazards

question: What does the 'slow-moving vehicle' symbol described in the manual look like?
choice_a: A red triangle with an orange center
choice_b: A yellow diamond with a black exclamation point
choice_c: An orange circle with black stripes
choice_d: A blue square with white lettering
explanation: The manual describes the slow-moving vehicle symbol: "This is a red triangle with an orange center. Watch for it."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards - Slow Drivers

question: When approaching a stopped authorized emergency vehicle or work zone, what does the manual say to do if a safe lane change is not possible?
choice_a: Stop completely on the shoulder until the scene clears
choice_b: Slow down and proceed with caution while maintaining a safe speed for traffic conditions
choice_c: Maintain your current speed but honk your horn
choice_d: Accelerate past quickly to minimize time near the hazard
explanation: The manual states, "If a lane change is unsafe, slow down and proceed with caution while maintaining a safe speed for traffic conditions."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.8.2 Hazardous Roads - Move-Over Laws

question: Why does the manual identify vans, loaded station wagons, and rental trucks as hazards?
choice_a: They are statistically more likely to be uninsured
choice_b: They are usually driven by inexperienced teenagers
choice_c: Their drivers' vision may be blocked to the sides and rear, or the driver may not be used to that limited vision
choice_d: They are exempt from vehicle inspection requirements
explanation: The manual notes, "People who can't see others are a very dangerous hazard... Vans, loaded station wagons, and cars with the rear window blocked are examples. Rental trucks should be watched carefully. Their drivers are often not used to the limited vision they have."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards - Blocked Vision

question: According to the manual, when are you 'in conflict' with another road user?
choice_a: Whenever you are behind another vehicle
choice_b: Only when a collision has already occurred
choice_c: Whenever another driver signals a turn
choice_d: When you have to change speed and/or direction to avoid hitting someone
explanation: The manual states, "You are in conflict when you have to change speed and/or direction to avoid hitting someone."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards - Conflicts

question: Research cited in the manual found that dialing a mobile telephone while driving makes CMV drivers how many times more likely to be involved in a safety-critical event?
choice_a: 6 times greater
choice_b: 23.2 times greater
choice_c: 2 times greater
choice_d: 39 times greater
explanation: The manual states the odds of a safety-critical event are "6 times greater for CMV drivers who engage in dialing a mobile telephone while driving than for those who do not."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: The manual states texting while driving makes CMV drivers how many times more likely to be involved in a safety-critical event, compared to non-texting drivers?
choice_a: 6 times greater
choice_b: 23.2 times greater
choice_c: 4 times greater
choice_d: 60 times greater
explanation: The manual states, "the odds of being involved in a safety-critical event... is 23.2 times greater for CMV drivers who engage in texting while driving than for those who do not."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.9.5 Texting

question: Under the manual, how long is a CDL disqualified after two convictions of texting while operating a CMV within three years?
choice_a: 30 days
choice_b: 90 days
choice_c: 60 days
choice_d: 1 year
explanation: The manual states, "Disqualification is 60 days for the second offense within 3 years and 120 days for three or more offenses within 3 years."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.9.5 Texting

topic: Civil penalty for hand-held phone use
question: What is the maximum civil penalty a driver can face for a hand-held mobile telephone violation, per the manual?
explanation: The manual states violations "are subject to civil penalties imposed on such drivers, in an amount up to $2,750."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

topic: Time eyes off road while dialing
question: The manual notes that dialing drivers took their eyes off the forward roadway for an average of how long?
choice_a: 3.8 seconds
choice_b: 1 second
choice_c: 10 seconds
choice_d: 4.6 seconds
explanation: The manual states, "Dialing drivers took their eyes off the forward roadway for an average of 3.8 seconds." (4.6 seconds is the figure given for texting, not dialing.)
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: How does the manual distinguish 'road rage' from 'aggressive driving'?
choice_a: They are the same thing and used interchangeably
choice_b: Road rage is operating a vehicle with intent to do harm to others or physically assault a driver or their vehicle, while aggressive driving is operating selfishly and boldly without regard for others' safety
choice_c: Aggressive driving is a felony while road rage is a misdemeanor
choice_d: Road rage only applies to passenger vehicles, not CMVs
explanation: The manual defines aggressive driving as "operating a motor vehicle in a selfish, bold, or pushy manner, without regard for the rights or safety of others," while road rage is "operating a motor vehicle with the intent of doing harm to others or physically assaulting a driver or their vehicle."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.10.1 What Is It?

question: What is the manual's first recommendation when confronted by an aggressive driver?
choice_a: Speed up to get away as fast as possible
choice_b: Make eye contact to show confidence
choice_c: Make every attempt to get out of their way
choice_d: Pull over and confront the driver calmly
explanation: The manual states, "First and foremost, make every attempt to get out of their way."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.10.3 What You Should Do When Confronted by an Aggressive Driver

question: According to the manual, about how far can you see ahead with low beams versus high beams at night?
choice_a: 100 feet with low beams, 200 feet with high beams
choice_b: 500 feet with low beams, 1,000 feet with high beams
choice_c: 150 feet with low beams, 250 feet with high beams
choice_d: About 250 feet with low beams, about 350-500 feet with high beams
explanation: The manual states, "With low beams you can see ahead about 250 feet and with high beams about 350-500 feet."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.11.4 Vehicle Factors - Headlights

question: Within how many feet of an oncoming or followed vehicle should you dim your headlights, per the manual?
choice_a: 500 feet
choice_b: 100 feet
choice_c: 1,000 feet
choice_d: 50 feet
explanation: The manual states, "Dim your lights within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and when following another vehicle within 500 feet."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.11.5 Night Driving Procedures - Avoid Blinding Others

topic: Best advice for driving in fog
question: What is the manual's 'best advice' for driving in fog?
choice_a: Use your high beams for maximum visibility
choice_b: Don't drive; pull off the road into a rest area or truck stop until visibility improves
choice_c: Speed up to get through the fog bank quickly
choice_d: Follow closely behind another vehicle's taillights
explanation: The manual states, "The best advice for driving in fog is don't. It is preferable that you pull off the road into a rest area or truck stop until visibility is better."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.12 Driving in Fog

question: What lights does the manual recommend using in fog, even in daytime?
choice_a: High beam headlights only
choice_b: Parking lights only
choice_c: Low-beam headlights and fog lights
choice_d: Interior dome light left on
explanation: The manual advises to "Use low-beam headlights and fog lights for best visibility even in daytime."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.12 Driving in Fog

question: For winter driving, the manual reiterates that tires must have at least what tread depth in every major groove on front tires?
choice_a: 2/32 inch
choice_b: 6/32 inch
choice_c: 8/32 inch
choice_d: 4/32 inch
explanation: The manual states, "You must have at least 4/32 inch tread depth in every major groove on front tires and at least 2/32 inch on other tires."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.13.1 Vehicle Checks - Tires

question: According to the manual, what is a sign that ice has formed on the road while driving in winter?
choice_a: A lack of spray from other vehicles' tires
choice_b: Other vehicles driving faster than normal
choice_c: A sudden drop in engine temperature
choice_d: Increased tire noise
explanation: The manual states, "A lack of spray from other vehicles indicates ice has formed on the road."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.13.2 Driving - Check for Ice

question: What does the manual say about using the engine brake or speed retarder on slippery winter roads?
choice_a: They should be used more aggressively than normal for extra stopping power
choice_b: Don't use the engine brake or speed retarder, because they can cause the driving wheels to skid
choice_c: They have no effect on traction either way
choice_d: They are legally required in snow conditions
explanation: The manual instructs, "don't use the engine brake or speed retarder. (They can cause the driving wheels to skid on slippery surfaces.)"
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.13.2 Driving - Adjust Turning and Braking to Conditions

question: After driving through deep water and drying out wet brakes, what does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Immediately resume normal highway speed without testing
choice_b: Apply the parking brake only, never the service brakes
choice_c: Check behind you, then make a test stop when safe to make sure the brakes work well
choice_d: Pump the brakes rapidly at highway speed
explanation: The manual advises, "Make a test stop when safe to do so. Check behind to make sure no one is following, then apply the brakes to be sure they work well."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.13.2 Driving - Wet Brakes

topic: Tire inspection interval in hot weather
question: In very hot weather, how often does the manual recommend inspecting tires?
choice_a: Once per day
choice_b: Every 500 miles
choice_c: Every 4 hours
choice_d: Every two hours or every 100 miles
explanation: The manual states, "Inspect the tires every two hours or every 100 miles when driving in very hot weather."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.14.1 Vehicle Checks - Tires

question: What does the manual advise about letting air out of a hot tire to reduce pressure?
choice_a: Do not let air out, or the pressure will be too low when the tires cool off
choice_b: Always release air until the tire feels cool to the touch
choice_c: Release air only if the tire has run more than 200 miles
choice_d: It makes no difference either way
explanation: The manual states, "Air pressure increases with temperature. Do not let air out or the pressure will be too low when the tires cool off."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.14.1 Vehicle Checks - Tires

question: What distinguishes an 'active' railroad-highway crossing from a 'passive' one, per the manual?
choice_a: Active crossings have no traffic control device at all
choice_b: Active crossings have a traffic control device such as flashing red lights, with or without bells and gates, while passive crossings rely on signs and pavement markings with no such device
choice_c: Passive crossings are found only in cities
choice_d: Active crossings are only found on interstate highways
explanation: The manual states passive crossings have "no type of traffic control device," while active crossings have "a traffic control device installed at the crossing... including flashing red lights, with or without bells, and flashing red lights with bells and gates."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.15.1 Types of Crossings

topic: Advance warning sign at railroad crossings
question: What does the round, black-on-yellow advance warning sign at a railroad crossing tell you to do?
choice_a: Proceed at normal speed since the crossing is protected
choice_b: Stop immediately regardless of a train's presence
choice_c: Slow down, look and listen for the train, and be prepared to stop at the tracks if a train is coming
choice_d: Change lanes to avoid the crossing
explanation: The manual states the advance warning sign "tells you to slow down, look and listen for the train, and be prepared to stop at the tracks if a train is coming."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.15.2 Warning Signs and Devices - Advance Warning Signs

question: According to the manual, how long does it typically take a tractor-trailer unit to clear a single track versus a double track?
choice_a: At least 5 seconds for a single track, 8 seconds for a double track
choice_b: At least 20 seconds for a single track, 30 seconds for a double track
choice_c: At least 10 seconds for a single track, 12 seconds for a double track
choice_d: At least 14 seconds for a single track, more than 15 seconds for a double track
explanation: The manual states, "It takes a typical tractor-trailer unit at least 14 seconds to clear a single track and more than 15 seconds to clear a double track."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.15.5 Crossing the Tracks

question: What does the manual say about racing a train to a crossing?
choice_a: Never attempt it, because it is extremely difficult to judge an approaching train's speed
choice_b: It is acceptable if your vehicle can exceed 55 mph
choice_c: It is only dangerous at night
choice_d: It is safe if the crossing has no gates
explanation: The manual states, "Never attempt to race a train to a crossing. It is extremely difficult to judge the speed of an approaching train."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.15.3 Driving Procedures - Never Race a Train to a Crossing

topic: Double tracks require a double check
question: Why does the manual say 'double tracks require a double check'?
choice_a: Because double-track crossings always have malfunctioning signals
choice_b: Because a train on one track may hide a train on the other track, so you should look both ways before crossing
choice_c: Because double tracks require two separate stops
choice_d: Because insurance regulations require two inspections
explanation: The manual states, "a train on one track may hide a train on the other track. Look both ways before crossing."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.15.3 Driving Procedures - Double Tracks Require a Double Check

question: What does the manual say happens to brakes on a long downgrade if you rely on them too much instead of engine braking?
choice_a: Nothing; brakes are designed to withstand unlimited heat
choice_b: They will automatically self-adjust to compensate
choice_c: They can 'fade' from excessive heat, requiring harder and harder application until you cannot slow or stop
choice_d: They will lock up immediately and cause a skid
explanation: The manual states brakes "can fade or fail from excessive heat caused by using them too much and not relying on the engine braking effect," and that if fading continues, "you cannot slow down or stop at all."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.16.3 Brake Fading or Failure

topic: Proper braking technique on a downgrade
question: In the manual's example of proper braking technique on a downgrade with a 'safe' speed of 40 mph, how much do you let your speed drop before releasing the brakes?
choice_a: Down to 20 mph
choice_b: Down to 30 mph
choice_c: Down to 38 mph
choice_d: Down to approximately 5 mph below your safe speed (about 35 mph), releasing the brakes after roughly a three-second application
explanation: The manual describes applying the brakes until speed drops "approximately 5 mph below your 'safe' speed" (about a three-second application), then releasing until speed returns to the safe speed and repeating.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.16.4 Proper Braking Technique

topic: Selecting the right gear before a descent
question: What does the manual say about downshifting on a mountain grade?
choice_a: Shift to a low gear before starting down the grade; don't wait until your speed has already built up
choice_b: It is best to downshift halfway down the grade for smoother deceleration
choice_c: Automatic transmissions should always be forced into a lower gear at high speed for extra braking
choice_d: Gear selection does not matter as long as the brakes are in good condition
explanation: The manual states, "Shift the transmission to a low gear before starting down the grade. Do not try to downshift after your speed has already built up."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.16.2 Select the Right Gear Before Starting Down the Grade

question: What is the purpose of an escape ramp on a steep mountain downgrade, per the manual?
choice_a: To provide a shortcut around the mountain for slow vehicles
choice_b: To stop runaway vehicles safely without injuring drivers and passengers, using a long bed of loose, soft material
choice_c: To allow faster descent for empty trucks
choice_d: To automatically weigh vehicles before the grade
explanation: The manual states, "Escape ramps are made to stop runaway vehicles safely without injuring drivers and passengers. Escape ramps use a long bed of loose, soft material to slow a runaway vehicle."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.16.4 Proper Braking Technique - Escape Ramps

topic: Factors in selecting a safe downgrade speed
question: Which of the following is NOT listed by the manual as a factor in selecting a 'safe' speed for a downgrade?
choice_a: Total weight of the vehicle and cargo
choice_b: Steepness of the grade
choice_c: The color of the vehicle
choice_d: Road conditions and weather
explanation: The manual lists total weight of vehicle and cargo, length of grade, steepness of grade, road conditions, and weather as the factors for selecting a safe speed on a downgrade - vehicle color is not among them.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.16.1 Select a "Safe" Speed

topic: Fatigue - NTSB truck driver fatality study
question: According to the NTSB (1990) finding cited in the Wyoming CDL Manual, drowsy driving was probably the cause of what portion of crashes leading to a truck driver's death?
choice_a: More than half
choice_b: About one quarter
choice_c: Less than 10 percent
choice_d: Exactly one third
explanation: The manual states the NTSB reported that drowsy driving was probably the cause of more than half of crashes leading to a truck driver's death (NTSB, 1990).
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.11 Night Driving, Fatigue and Lack of Alertness

question: Per the Wyoming CDL Manual, approximately how many police-reported crashes a year does NHTSA estimate are the result of drowsy driving?
explanation: The manual states NHTSA estimates that 100,000 police-reported crashes a year are the result of drowsy driving.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.11 Night Driving, Fatigue and Lack of Alertness

topic: Fatigue - Sleep in America poll, driven while sleepy
question: According to the National Sleep Foundation's Sleep in America poll cited in the manual, what percentage of Americans have driven while feeling sleepy?
choice_a: 36 percent
choice_b: 15 percent
choice_c: 60 percent
choice_d: 40 percent
explanation: The manual states that 60 percent of Americans have driven while feeling sleepy, according to the National Sleep Foundation's Sleep in America poll.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.11 Night Driving, Fatigue and Lack of Alertness

topic: Fatigue - Sleep in America poll, fallen asleep at wheel
question: Per the same Sleep in America poll cited in the manual, what percentage of Americans admit to actually having fallen asleep at the wheel in the past year?
choice_a: 60 percent
choice_b: 15 percent
choice_c: 8 percent
choice_d: 36 percent
explanation: The manual states that 36 percent (or 103 million people) admit to having actually fallen asleep at the wheel in the past year.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.11 Night Driving, Fatigue and Lack of Alertness

topic: Fatigue - share of heavy truck crashes
question: Per the Wyoming CDL Manual, fatigue is involved in at least what percentage of all heavy truck crashes?
choice_a: 15 percent
choice_b: 5 percent
choice_c: 10 percent
choice_d: 25 percent
explanation: The manual states that at least 15 percent of all heavy truck crashes involve fatigue.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.11 Night Driving, Fatigue and Lack of Alertness

question: The congressionally mandated FMCSA study of 80 long-haul truck drivers cited in the manual found that drivers averaged how much sleep per day?
choice_a: 8 to 9 hours
choice_b: Less than 5 hours
choice_c: About 7 hours
choice_d: More than 6 hours
explanation: The manual states the study found that drivers averaged less than 5 hours of sleep per day (Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, 1996).
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.11 Night Driving, Fatigue and Lack of Alertness

topic: Fatigue - effect of sleep deprivation on risk
question: Per the manual's 'Are You at Risk' list, getting 6 hours of sleep or less before driving has what effect on your crash risk?
choice_a: It doubles your risk
choice_b: It has no significant effect on risk
choice_c: It triples your risk
choice_d: It reduces your risk by half
explanation: The manual lists being sleep-deprived or fatigued, defined as 6 hours of sleep or less, as tripling your crash risk.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.11 Night Driving, Are You at Risk

question: According to the manual's 'Are You at Risk' list, working more than 60 hours a week increases your fatigue-related crash risk by what percentage?
choice_a: 10 percent
choice_b: 25 percent
choice_c: 60 percent
choice_d: 40 percent
explanation: The manual states that working more than 60 hours a week increases your risk by 40 percent.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.11 Night Driving, Are You at Risk

topic: Fatigue - the only safe cure for drowsiness
question: If you become drowsy while driving, what does the Wyoming CDL Manual say is the only safe cure?
choice_a: Get off the road and get some sleep
choice_b: Drink coffee or another caffeinated beverage
choice_c: Open the window for fresh air
choice_d: Turn on the radio or air conditioning
explanation: The manual states, "If you are drowsy, the only safe cure is to get off the road and get some sleep. If you don't, you risk your life and the lives of others."
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.11 Night Driving, Fatigue and Lack of Alertness

topic: Fatigue - recommended sleep to maintain alertness
question: Per the manual's guidance on preventing drowsiness before a trip, how many hours of sleep do adults need to maintain alertness?
choice_a: 5 to 6 hours
choice_b: 8 to 9 hours
choice_c: 10 to 11 hours
choice_d: 6 to 7 hours
explanation: The manual advises getting adequate sleep, stating adults need 8 to 9 hours to maintain alertness.
source_note: Wyoming CDL Manual (Oct 2024), Section 2 - subsection 2.11 Night Driving, Preventing Drowsiness Before a Trip
